ety.text: Proto-Indo-European *kap-der. Proto-Germanic *habjaną Proto-West Germanic *habbjan Old English habban Middle English haven English have From Middle English haven, from Old English habban (“to have”), from Proto-West Germanic *habbjan, from Proto-Germanic *habjaną (“to have”), durative of *habjaną (“to lift, take up”), from Proto-Indo-European *kapyéti, an imperfective formation to the root *kap- (“to take, seize, catch”). Related to heave.
From have on (“to deceive”).
Variant of haw.

senses.d: To possess, own.
ex: I have a house and a car.

senses.d: To hold, as something at someone's disposal.
ex: Look what I have here—a frog I found on the street!
Do you have the key?

senses.d: To include as a part, ingredient, or feature.
ex: The stove has a handle. The shirt has sleeves.
The words cow and dog have three letters.

senses.d: Used to state the existence or presence of someone in a specified relationship with the subject.
ex: I have two sisters.
She doesn’t have any friends.

senses.d: To consume or use up (a particular substance or resource, especially food or drink).
ex: I have breakfast at six o'clock.
You've already had five drinks!

senses.d: To undertake or perform (an action or activity).
ex: Can I have a look at that?
He's having a tantrum about it.

senses.d: To be scheduled to attend, undertake or participate in.
ex: What class do you have right now? I have English.
Fred won’t be able to come to the party; he has a meeting that day.

senses.d: To experience, go through, undergo.
ex: We had a hard year last year, with the locust swarms and all that.
He had surgery on his hip yesterday.

senses.d: To be afflicted with, suffer from.
ex: He had a cold last week.

senses.d: Used in forming the perfect aspect.
ex: I have already eaten today.
Mom's gone real mad, she has.

senses.d: A wealthy or privileged person.
ex: A good credit rating can mean the difference between being a have or a have not.

senses.d: One who has some (contextually specified) thing.
A fraud or deception; something misleading.
ex: They advertise it as a great deal, but I think it's a bit of a have.

senses.d: A hawthorn.

ety.text: From Middle English havok, havyk, from Old French havok in the phrase crier havok (“cry havoc”) a signal to soldiers to seize plunder, from Old French crier (“cry out, shout”) + havot (“pillaging, looting”), of obscure origin. Probably from a derivative of Old French *haf, hef (“hook”), from Frankish *haf, *habbjā, *happjā (“pruning-hook, scythe”), derived from Proto-Germanic *habjaną (“to take up, lift”), related to Old French havee (“handful”), Old French havet (“pruning-hook”), Old High German habba, heppa (“pruning-hook, scythe”), modern German Hippe (“billhook”).
